title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E410, §§X–XII): Euler treats a plane thread or rod element Mm of length ds. At the cross-section M it carries a tangential force T (tension) and a normal force V (shear). The normal force acts along a line VP at lever arm v from m. At m the corresponding forces are T+dT and V+dV, with lever arm v+dv. External loads per unit length are p (tangential) and q (normal). The contingence angle is dΦ = ds/r. On the previous page Euler resolved the forces at m along the tangent mT and the normal. On this page he writes the three equilibrium conditions of the element.

(1) Tangential balance: T + dT + V dΦ + dV dΦ = T + p ds. Dropping second-order terms gives dT + V dΦ = p ds.

(2) Normal balance: −(T+dT)dΦ + (V+dV) = V + q ds, giving dV − T dΦ = q ds.

(3) Moments about m: (V+dV)(v+dv) = V(v+ds). The terms in T dΦ and q ds have zero arm. This gives v dV + V dv = V ds, i.e. d(Vv) = V ds.

In modern terms, with M = Vv the bending moment:
- N' + κQ = p
- Q' − κN = q
- M' = Q

These are the planar Kirchhoff–Clebsch equilibrium equations of a rod without distributed couples. Euler says these three equations contain everything needed. In §XII he announces two specialisations:
- the perfectly flexible thread: V = 0, giving dT = p ds and −T dΦ = q ds;
- the uniformly elastic lamina: on the next page he sets Vv = A dΦ/ds, the Bernoulli–Euler constitutive law.

The point of the page is the general one-dimensional balance law including shear force, from which both the catenary-type and the elastica-type theories follow.
errors: As printed, the normal-force equation reads −(T+dT)dΦ + dV = V + q ds; the left side should contain V + dV. The derived result dV − T dΦ = q ds is correct, so this is a typographical omission in the original.
Second-order products (dV·dΦ, dT·dΦ, dV·dv) are dropped without comment. This is standard and legitimate.
The moment equation tacitly assumes no distributed external couples and that the load q ds acts at m (zero arm). Both are acceptable to first order.

ideas.what: Balance of tangential and normal forces on a curved line element including a shear (normal) force V
ideas.modern_name: Planar rod equilibrium equations N' + κQ = p, Q' − κN = q (Kirchhoff–Clebsch / Cosserat rod equations, plane case)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E410 (1771), as identified by Truesdell (1960), building on James Bernoulli and Euler's earlier elastica work
ideas.where_published: E410, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 15 (1771); Opera omnia II.11; analysed in Truesdell, 'The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788' (O.O. II.11₂)

ideas.what: Moment balance of the element giving d(Vv) = V ds, i.e. shear force equals the derivative of the bending moment
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E410 (moment balance as an independent principle; cf. E479 for the general statement)

ideas.what: Reduction to the perfectly flexible case (V = 0) and to the elastic case (Vv = A dΦ/ds)
ideas.modern_name: String equilibrium equations; Bernoulli–Euler constitutive law for the elastica
ideas.where_published: E410; earlier E65 Additamentum I (1744) for the elastica

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known core of E410: Euler's general plane rod equations with shear force and a separate moment balance. Truesdell treated it at length as a landmark. Nothing on the page is absent from the historical record.
transcription_corrections: Second equation: the transcription faithfully reproduces the printed '−(T + dT) dΦ + dV = V + qds'. Mathematically the left side should read −(T+dT)dΦ + V + dV, a typo in the original rather than in the transcription.
